extracted.intended_audience: English citizens and the reform-minded public (readers interested in government, politics, and national reform)
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century political pamphlet arguing criteria for good government, peaceful reform versus violent revolution, concrete fiscal and military reforms, and principles for religion and publishing. It addresses how nations should assess and pursue reforms and the indicators of good government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of a good constitution and government
rubrics_metrics.description: “When it shall be said in any country in the world, my poor are happy; neither ignorance nor distress is to be found among them; my jails are empty of prisoners, my streets of beggars; the aged are not in want, the taxes are not oppressive; the rational world is my friend, because I am the friend of its happiness: when these things can be said, then may that country boast its constitution and its government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions are presented as substantive measures by which a nation may claim its constitution and government are worthy; they function as evaluative criteria for governments (poverty, education, incarceration, public charity, taxation, and international reputation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions should be driven by reason and common interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “From both those instances it is evident, that the greatest forces that can be brought into the field of revolutions, are reason and common interest. Where these can have the opportunity of acting, opposition dies with fear, or crumbles away by conviction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates peaceful, deliberative change: reforms achieved by public reason and shared interest are preferable and more effective than force; this is presented as a principle for evaluating means of political change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use force when reform can be achieved by reason
rubrics_metrics.description: “it would not only be wrong, but bad policy, to attempt by force what ought to be accomplished by reason.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescription and evaluative rule: prefer persuasion, discussion, and accommodation over violent methods unless peaceful avenues are suppressed; anti-pattern is precipitating violent revolt where deliberative mechanisms suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for methods to ascertain public opinion (national conventions / representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There ought, therefore, to be in every nation a method of occasionally ascertaining the state of public opinion with respect to government... the old government of France was superior ... because, on extraordinary occasions, recourse could be had what was then called the States General.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that institutions (e.g., national conventions or properly functioning representatives) should periodically reveal the people's will; critiques existing English representation as largely captive to court influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of the people to convene for general reform
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is, therefore, no power but the voluntary right of the people that has a right to act in any matter respecting a general reform; and by the same right that two persons can confer on such a subject, a thousand may.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts a broad procedural/political right: collective popular assemblies or conventions may be formed to deliberate reforms; this functions as a normative standard for legitimacy of reform efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule must not impose unequal conditions on minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: “so long as the majority do not impose conditions on the minority, different from what they impose upon themselves, though there may be much error, there is no injustice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets a fairness constraint on democratic decisions: majority decisions can be erroneous yet not unjust if they treat minorities under the same rules the majority accepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between active and passive revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: “In contemplating revolutions, it is easy to perceive that they may arise from two distinct causes; the one, to avoid or get rid of some great calamity; the other, to obtain some great and positive good; and the two may be distinguished by the names of active and passive revolutions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative framework: active (reactive to calamity) revolutions tend to be vindictive and disorderly; passive (aimed at achieving positive good) are calmer, guided by reason and persuasion; prefer passive when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer passive/reformist processes to violent upheaval
rubrics_metrics.description: “In those which proceed from the latter cause, the heart, rather animated than agitated, enters serenely upon the subject. Reason and discussion, persuasion and conviction, become the weapons in the contest, and it is only when those are attempted to be suppressed that recourse is had to violence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for political strategy and assessment of movements: evaluate reforms positively if they are pursued by persuasion; violent methods are only justified (if at all) by suppression of peaceful avenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confederated naval disarmament proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: “if the fleets of England, France, and Holland were confederated, they could propose, with effect, a limitation to, and a general dismantling of, all the navies in Europe, to a certain proportion to be agreed upon. First, That no new ship of war shall be built by any power in Europe, themselves included. Second, That all the navies now in existence shall be put back, suppose to one-tenth of their present force.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete international policy prescription with fiscal and security rationales: a multilateral naval limitation would save large sums and reduce arms races; presented as a practical reform rather than mere idealism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use international alliances to open markets and promote independence
rubrics_metrics.description: “the above confederated powers, together with that of the United States of America, can propose with effect, to Spain, the independence of South America, and the opening those countries of immense extent and wealth to the general commerce of the world...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic criterion: alliance-building can be used to promote independence movements and expand commerce; evaluated in terms of economic benefit and reduction of burdens on nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace is more advantageous than war; war serves government interests
rubrics_metrics.description: “Peace, which costs nothing, is attended with infinitely more advantage, than any victory with all its expense. But this, though it best answers the purpose of nations, does not that of court governments, whose habited policy is pretence for taxation, places, and offices. But any war is harvest to such governments, however ruinous it may be to a nation. It serves to keep up deceitful expectations which prevent people from looking into the defects and abuses of government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative evaluation of foreign policy: favor peaceful arrangements and beware of wars that sustain corrupt governmental interests and hidden taxation motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific tax and poor-relief proposals as measures of reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed remissions and support: “a remission of five pounds annually of taxes to one hundred and four thousand poor families... seven pounds annually to one hundred thousand other poor families... eight pounds annually to another hundred thousand poor families, and of ten pounds annually to fifty thousand poor and widowed families... securing six pounds annually for all poor, distressed, and reduced persons of the age of fifty and until sixty, and of ten pounds annually after sixty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete fiscal measures and social-welfare benchmarks offered as part of a reform plan; these figures function as prescriptive criteria for measuring the generosity and fairness of tax relief and poor relief policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish oppressive taxes and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “Will he say that an abolition of two millions of poor-rates to the house-keepers, and of the whole of the house and window-light tax and of the commutation tax is not a good thing? Or will he say that to abolish corruption is a bad thing?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and moral criterion: eliminating specific regressive taxes and systemic corruption is presented as an unequivocal improvement and standard for evaluating fiscal reform proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane treatment and discharge of soldiers; avoid maintaining unnecessary standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: “It would be better that nations should wi continue the pay of their soldiers during their lives, and give them their discharge and restore them to freedom and their friends, and cease recruiting, than retain such multitudes at the same expense, in a condition useless to society and to themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veterans’ policy standard: prioritize discharge and reintegration with continued support over ongoing recruitment and maintenance of large standing forces; evaluates military policy by social utility and humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government fosters international acquaintance and peace
rubrics_metrics.description: “When all the governments of Europe shall be established on the representative system, nations will become acquainted, and the animosities and prejudices fomented by the intrigue and artifice of courts, will cease.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional criterion: representative systems are evaluated as instruments for reducing international animosity and improving safety of commerce and citizens; used to justify domestic constitutional reform as having international benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion should not be made a political machine; evaluate religions by moral teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: “Throughout this work, various and numerous as the subjects are, which I have taken up and investigated, there is only a single paragraph upon religion, viz. 'that every religion is good that teaches man to be good.' ... But as religion is very improperly made a political machine, and the reality of it is thereby destroyed... If we suppose a large family of children... The parent would be more gratified by such a variety... Why may we not suppose, that the great Father of all is pleased with variety of devotion; and that the greatest offence we can act, is that by which we seek to torment and render each other miserable?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative principle: judge religions by their moral effect (teaching goodness); oppose state-established national religions and political exploitation of religion; support freedom and variety in devotional expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should retain control of their copy to prevent suppression and alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix account: the printer returned the remaining copy without warning, after previously offering to buy copyright and after apparent opportunities for ministerial booksellers to view proofs; the author refused offers to sell copyright to prevent suppression or alteration of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive norm for publishing ethics and authorial integrity: an author should not relinquish control in ways that permit suppression or unauthorized alteration; transparency about publication timing and custody of proofs is relevant evidence when evaluating claims of suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of circumstantial evidence to evaluate possible suppression or collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix: Paine lists timing of proofs, printer's conduct, offers, and the involvement of a ministerial bookseller as 'suspicious circumstances' though he declines to make formal accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion: when investigating possible suppression or prior access to manuscripts, evaluate chain-of-custody, timing of proofs, offers to purchase, and proximity of politically connected publishers as relevant indicators.
